Q: For a Combine Publisher operator, how can be designed safe for concurrency? A:

In general, yes, a subscriber will generally receive it on the same thread as it was published, but there are not, AFAIK, any formal assurances to that effect. Generally this is a non-issue and if you need to get the values from a particular publisher on a particular thread, you would use receive(on:options:).

But you then reference “concurrency safe”. That term generally applies to Swift concurrency (async-await, actors, etc.). The concurrency-safety we achieve in Swift concurrency is achieved through actor-isolation (and all the wonderful compile-time checks that “strict concurrency checking” affords us). But Combine predates Swift concurrency. Swift concurrency’s actor-isolation rules generally don’t apply to legacy code that isn’t employing actor-isolation at all, such as Combine. In Combine (and GCD code), we bear the responsibility for ensuring “thread safety” (not “concurrency safety”) and use legacy runtime tools like TSAN or the like, to verify that our code is thread safe. The burden for ensuring that our legacy code is safe from data races rests on our shoulders (which, needless to say, can be brittle).

So, with our Combine pipelines, the burden to ensure, for example, that our publisher (or something else) doesn’t subsequently mutate some object after publishing it (i.e., introducing potential “data races”) rests on our shoulders. Generally this is a non-issue, as most publishers instantiate objects, publish them, and forget them (i.e., the publisher generally doesn’t mutate objects again after publishing them). We generally try to follow this pattern in our own publishers and it keeps life quite simple (albeit, without the compile-time guardrails that Swift concurrency affords us).

Now, you then discuss the problem of how to achieve “concurrency safety” (by which I assume you really are talking about achieving “thread safety”) and introducing OperationQueue to accomplish this. I guess I could contrive of examples where one might contemplate that, but it’s generally simply not necessary. I might suggest you provide a MRE of a Combine pipeline where you felt compelled to reach for OperationQueue. (Perhaps you can share the simple pipeline, before any OperationQueue stuff was added.) Generally, I would be inclined to use receive(on:options:) on a dispatch queue for my Publisher, not an operation queue. Maybe you can show us what problem you were trying to solve with the OperationQueue and we might be able to advise better ways to achieve the desired thread-safe behavior.

Note: OperationQueue, like DispatchQueue, conforms to Scheduler. So, if you’re using a serial OperationQueue (i.e., one with maxConcurrentOperationCount of 1) in receive(on:options:), then that’s a fine pattern, too. That having been said, I would still lean towards DispatchQueue, unless you had some compelling reason to prefer an OperationQueue.

Q: How to end or fail AWS Glue job with error? A:

Unfortunately, there's no built-in API in AWS Glue to gracefully exit with a failure status without throwing an exception. The Glue service determines job Status based on how the job terminates:

  • Normal exit -> SUCCEEDED

  • Exception thrown -> FAILED

Recommended Approach

Throw a Custom Business Exception

Create a dedicated exception for controlled failures: this gives you a clean error message in the Glue console:

// Define a custom exception for business logic failures
class GlueJobValidationException(message: String) extends Exception(message)

// Usage
val input = glueContext
  .getCataglogSource(database = "my_db", tableName = "my_table")
  .getDynamicFrame()

val myLimit = 10
if (input.count() <= my Limit) {
  throw new GlueJobValidationException(
    s"Job terminated: Input recourd count (${input.count()}) is below minimum threshold ($myLimit)"
  )
}

This will:

  • Mark the job as FAILED

  • Show your custom message in CloudWatch and Glue console

  • Provide a clear, readable error (not a cryptic stack trace)

Q: Why my navigation items are not visible into my bootstrap navigation bar? A:

The navigation has disappeared because the collapse class has been applied to the navigation container, and it has the style visibility: collapse, that's why it has disappeared.

If you remove the CSS or override it with new CSS, the issue is resolved.

CSS: .navbar-expand-lg .navbar-collapse {visibility: visible !important;}
